projects.title: UWASIC
projects.subtitle: Digital design, from RTL to layout.
projects.summary: Designing functional-unit RTL for Waterloo’s ray-tracing ASIC, building on a completed SPI/PWM onboarding project.

cover.alt: Top-down view of the chip layout: rows of standard cells crossed by vertical power straps, with the routed SPI and PWM logic concentrated in the upper half.
cover.caption: GDS layout of my SPI/PWM onboarding design, shown in a 3D layout viewer.

overview: I’m an RTL design member of UWASIC, the University of Waterloo’s chip design team. My current work is functional-unit RTL for a ray-tracing ASIC, collaborating with the verification team toward passing functional tests and a lint-clean RTL-to-GDS flow.

Before that work, I completed a digital-design onboarding project: a Verilog SPI Mode 0 peripheral with register-controlled outputs and PWM. That project connected RTL implementation, automated verification, and physical-layout generation.

sections.title: The peripheral
body: The onboarding peripheral has five registers and sixteen outputs. I implemented SPI Mode 0 communication and two-stage clock-domain crossing to move signals between clock domains.
bullets: Verilog RTL for the SPI peripheral and output controls.
Register interface for configuring peripheral behavior.
Two-stage CDC for signals crossing clock domains.

sections.title: Verification & tooling
body: I wrote Python/cocotb tests for 3 kHz PWM, checking 0%, 50%, and 100% duty cycles as well as output-enable behavior. I configured Tiny Tapeout and GitHub Actions to run simulation tests and generate GDS layout files.

sections.title: Current work
body: I’m now applying that foundation to functional-unit RTL for UWASIC’s ray-tracing ASIC. This is ongoing team work; the completed peripheral and its verification flow are the onboarding portion of the project.

outcome: Completed the SPI/PWM onboarding project with automated simulation tests and GDS generation. The next stage is continuing functional-unit design and verification with the UWASIC team.

projects.title: SignEd
projects.subtitle: A more hands-on way to learn ASL.
projects.summary: An interactive ASL learning website that connects live hand-pose recognition with guided lessons.

cover.alt: The five-person SignEd team standing in front of a projected slide that reads “1st Place Winner, Beginner Tier, $650, SignEd”, most of them making the ASL “I love you” sign.
cover.caption: Our team after SignEd won first place in the Beginner Track at Hack the Bias.

overview: SignEd is an ASL learning website built for Hack the Bias. As the team’s sole programmer, I developed the application using Python, Flask, JavaScript, and HTML/CSS, connecting computer vision to an interactive learning experience.

sections.title: Recognizing a sign
body: MediaPipe and OpenCV provide the hand-tracking pipeline. I normalized 21 three-dimensional hand landmarks by wrist position and hand size, then used distance-weighted K-nearest neighbors to recognize ASL poses.

sections.title: Connecting recognition to learning
body: Live recognition feedback is connected to guided lessons. A learner unlocks progression after holding the correct sign for three seconds, connecting the recognition result to a clear practice goal.

sections.title: My contribution
bullets: Implemented the Python/Flask application and the browser interface.
Built the hand-landmark normalization and pose-classification pipeline.
Connected live feedback to lesson progression.

outcome: SignEd won the Beginner Track at Hack the Bias. The project brought together computer vision, a web interface, and guided practice in one ASL learning experience.

projects.title: VEX Robotics
projects.subtitle: Build. Test. Tune. Compete.
projects.summary: A VEX V5 competition robot, from mechanical design and autonomous routines to the 2023 World Championship.
overview: I designed and built a VEX V5 competition robot and programmed its autonomous routines. My work covered the drivetrain, disc intake, and flywheel launcher, with repeated testing and mechanical adjustments between iterations.

sections.title: Mechanical design
body: I designed and built the drivetrain, intake, and flywheel launcher. These systems needed to work together to move around the field, collect discs, and launch them consistently.

sections.title: Testing & iteration
body: I iteratively tuned flywheel speed and intake spacing to improve shooting consistency and reduce jams. This work connected observations on the field with changes to the mechanism and its settings.

sections.title: Autonomous routines
body: Alongside the mechanical work, I programmed the robot’s autonomous routines. The project combined robot construction, programming, and competition testing.

outcome: Our team placed second in Alberta Provincial Robot Skills and qualified for the VEX Robotics World Championship. We competed in Dallas in 2023.

projects.title: C++ Ray Tracer
projects.subtitle: Following light, one ray at a time.
projects.summary: A C++ path tracer exploring ray geometry, diffuse shading, and the trade-off between image noise and render time.
overview: I built a C++ path tracer using the framework from Ray Tracing in One Weekend. This was a learning project focused on understanding how geometric intersections and repeated light sampling turn a scene into an image.

sections.title: Geometry & intersections
body: I implemented parametric rays, ray-sphere intersections, and surface normals. These establish where a ray meets the scene and the orientation of the surface at that point.

sections.title: Shading & sampling
body: I implemented Monte Carlo diffuse shading and multisample anti-aliasing to render spheres with smoother edges and reduced image noise.

sections.title: Quality versus rendering time
body: I analyzed how samples per pixel affect image noise and rendering time. This made sampling a practical trade-off to investigate as well as a part of the rendering algorithm.

outcome: Built a working C++ path tracer and explored the relationship between geometry, shading, sampling, and image quality. The implementation follows the educational framework of Ray Tracing in One Weekend.

projects.title: Calgary Ace Learning Center
projects.subtitle: Learning together. Giving back.
projects.summary: A student-run nonprofit bringing together tutoring, volunteer organizing, and fundraising for children’s healthcare.

highlights.label: Raised for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation

overview: I co-founded Calgary Ace Learning Center, a student-run nonprofit. My work focuses on tutoring, organizing, and fundraising: contributing time to help students learn while supporting a cause beyond the classroom.

sections.title: Teaching & volunteering
body: I have contributed more than 400 volunteer hours through tutoring and organizing. Teaching is a central part of my involvement, alongside the work needed to help a student-run organization operate.

sections.title: Fundraising for children’s healthcare
body: I led fundraising that raised more than $5,000 for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation. This work connected our student-led organization with a broader community purpose.

sections.title: Building the organization
body: As a co-founder, I contribute to both the educational work and the organization behind it. I also built its WordPress website to support its online presence.

outcome: An ongoing commitment to education and community service, with more than 400 volunteer hours contributed and $5,000+ raised for the Alberta Children’s Hospital Foundation.
